passages.original: Non est passus Agamemnon me diutius declamare in porticu, quam ipse in schola sudaverat, sed “Adulescens” inquit “quoniam sermonem habes non publici saporis et, quod rarissimum est, amas bonam mentem, non fraudabo te arte secreta. Nihil nimirum in his exercitationibus doctores peccant, qui necesse habent cum insanientibus furere. Nam nisi dixerint quae adulescentuli probent, ut ait Cicero, 'soli in scholis relinquentur.' Sicut ficti adulatores cum cenas divitum captant, nihil prius meditantur quam id quod putant gratissi mum auditoribus fore: nec enim aliter impetrabunt quod petunt, nisi quasdam insidias auribus fecerint: sic eloquentiae magister, nisi tanquam piscator eam imposuerit hamis escam, quam scierit appetituros esse pisciculos, sine spe praedae morabitur in scopulo.
passages.english: Agamemnon did not allow me to declaim in the portico longer than he himself had sweated in the school, but said, "Young man, since you have a way of speaking that is not to the common taste and, what is very rare, you love good sense, I will not cheat you of a secret of the craft. Of course the teachers are not at all to blame in these exercises, since they are obliged to rave along with the madmen. For unless they say what the young lads approve, as Cicero says, 'they will be left alone in the schools.' Just as the flatterers in comedy, when they angle for the dinners of the rich, think of nothing before what they suppose will be most pleasing to their listeners (for they will not get what they are after unless they lay some sort of trap for the ears), so a master of eloquence, unless, like a fisherman, he puts on his hooks the bait he knows the little fish will go for, will sit on his rock with no hope of a catch.
passages.notes: 'ficti adulatores' taken as the stock flatterers (parasites) of comedy; literally 'feigned flatterers'. 'gratissi mum' read as 'gratissimum'.

passages.original: si factum non est, nihil est.” Haec aliaque cum effusissimis prosequeremur laudationibus, “Rogo” inquit “Agamemnon mihi carissime, numquid duodecim aerumnas Herculis tenes, aut de Vlixe fabulam, quemadmodum illi Cyclops pollicem forcipe extorsit? Solebam haec ego puer apud Homerum legere. Nam Sibyllam quidem Cumis ego ipse oculis meis vidi in ampulla pendere, et cum illi pueri dicerent: Si/bulla, ti/ qe/leis; respondebat illa: a)poqanei=n qe/lw.”
passages.english: if it did not happen, it is nothing." While we were following these and other remarks with the most lavish praise, he said, "Tell me, my dearest Agamemnon, do you remember the twelve labours of Hercules, or the story about Ulysses, how the Cyclops wrenched out his thumb with pincers? I used to read these things in Homer as a boy. For I myself saw with my own eyes the Sibyl at Cumae hanging in a jar, and when the boys said to her, 'Sibyl, what do you want?' she answered, 'I want to die.'"
passages.notes: The Sibyl's exchange is in Greek in the original (transliterated in the edition's beta code). Trimalchio's mythology is deliberately garbled (the Cyclops and the thumb are not in Homer).

passages.original: ” ab hoc epigrammate coepit poetarum esse mentio diuque summa carminis penes Mopsum Thracem memorata est done Trimalchio “Rogo” inquit "magister, quid putas inter Ciceronem et Publilium interesse? Ego alterum puto disertiorem fuisse, alterum honestiorem. Quid enim his melius dici potest? “
passages.english: From this epigram talk turned to poets, and for a long time the top prize for poetry was assigned to Mopsus the Thracian, until Trimalchio said, "Tell me, teacher, what do you think is the difference between Cicero and Publilius? I think the one was more eloquent, the other more decent. For what can be said better than these lines?
passages.notes: 'done' read as 'donec'. 'Mopsus the Thracian' is unidentified; the text here is often considered corrupt (possibly a garbled reference to Orpheus or a play on a name). Publilius is presumably Publilius Syrus, the mime-writer.

passages.original: “Videbatur mihi secundum quietem Priapus dicere: 'Encolpion quod quaeris, scito a me in navem tuam esse perductum.” ' Exhorruit Tryphaena et “Putes” inquit “una nos dormiisse; nam et mihi simulacrum Neptuni, quod Baiis in tetrastylo notaveram, videbatur dicere: in nave Lichae Gitona invenies.'” “Hinc scies” inquit Eumolpus “Epicurum esse hominem divinum, qui eiusmodi ludibria facetissima ratione condemnat” ceterum Lichas ut Tryphaenae somnium expiavit,“quis” inquit “prohibet navigium scrutari, ne videamur divinae mentis opera damnare?” Is qui nocte miserorum furtum deprehenderat, Hesus nomine, subito proclamat: “Ergo illi qui sunt, qui nocte ad lunam radebantur pessimo medius fidius exemplo?
passages.english: "It seemed to me in my sleep that Priapus said: 'Encolpius, whom you are looking for, know that he has been brought by me onto your ship.'" Tryphaena shuddered and said, "You would think we had slept together; for to me too the statue of Neptune, which I had noticed in the four-columned portico at Baiae, seemed to say: 'You will find Giton on Lichas' ship.'" "From this you will see," said Eumolpus, "that Epicurus was a godlike man, who condemns mockeries of this kind with a most witty argument." But Lichas, after he had made expiation for Tryphaena's dream, said, "Who forbids us to search the ship, so that we do not seem to scorn the workings of the divine mind?" The man who had caught the poor wretches in their secret act during the night, Hesus by name, suddenly cried out: "So who are those people who were being shaved at night by the moonlight, a very bad precedent, so help me God?
passages.notes: 'Is qui nocte miserorum furtum deprehenderat': 'furtum' taken as 'secret/stealthy act'.
